blocks.text: Recursive functions come in a few shapes, and the shape decides how much time and memory they need. The useful way to see any recursion is its **call tree**: each call is a node, and the calls it makes are its children. Running the function **walks that tree depth-first** — all the way down the first branch, back up, then down the next.

blocks.alt: The call tree of fib(4). fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2); fib(3) calls fib(2) and fib(1); each fib(2) calls fib(1) and fib(0). The small numbers show the order the calls run: depth-first, left before right, 1 to 9. The green numbers are the values each call returns. fib(2) is computed twice — the waste dynamic programming removes.

items: **Linear recursion** — each call makes **one** recursive call: factorial, sum of a list, reversing a string. The call tree is a single path: **n calls, depth n**.

**Tail recursion** — linear recursion where the call is the **last** thing the function does, carrying the answer in a parameter. Could run in O(1) space, but JavaScript, Python and Java don't optimise it.

**Tree (multiple) recursion** — each call makes **two or more** calls: Fibonacci, generating subsets, most backtracking. The tree **branches**, so calls grow exponentially — **b^depth** for b branches — while memory is still just the depth.
**Divide and conquer** — split the input into parts, solve each part recursively, combine: merge sort, quick sort, binary search, fast power. Halving each time keeps the depth to **log n**.
**Mutual recursion** — two functions that call each other, like `isEven(n)` calling `isOdd(n − 1)`. Parsers for nested expressions work this way.

blocks.text: The order the call tree is walked
Every call tree is walked **depth-first**. What changes is **when** a call does its own work relative to its recursive calls — exactly like pre-order and post-order traversals of a binary tree:

items: **Work before the call (pre-order, "head")** — the work happens on the way **down**, so it comes out in calling order.

**Work after the call (post-order)** — the work waits until the call returns, so it happens on the way **back up**, in reverse order. Combining children's answers (fib, merge sort, tree heights) is always post-order.

blocks.text: The same function prints 3, 2, 1 or 1, 2, 3 depending only on where the line sits:

blocks.code:
def count_up(n, out=None):
    out = [] if out is None else out
    if n == 0:
        return out
    count_up(n - 1, out)          # the call first ...
    out.append(n)                 # ... then the work: comes out last
    return out

blocks.caption: Watch the call tree grow depth-first, and notice the same small calls being solved again and again.

blocks.text: Time and memory at a glance

blocks.code:
shape                   example          calls (time)        depth (stack memory)
linear                  factorial(n)     n                   n
tree, 2 branches        fib(n)           about 1.6^n         n
divide and conquer      merge sort       about 2n            log n
halving, one branch     binary search    log n               log n
backtracking            subsets of n     2^n                 n

blocks.text: Two rules cover almost everything: **time ≈ number of calls × work per call**, and **space ≈ maximum depth × memory per frame** (plus anything you store).

items: Draw the **call tree**: its size is the time, its height is the stack memory.
Linear recursion is a path; tree recursion branches and grows exponentially; divide and conquer stays log n deep.
The tree is always walked depth-first; work **before** the calls happens top-down, work **after** happens bottom-up.
Repeated subtrees, like fib(2) above, are the signal for dynamic programming.
